title: Kubernetes operators: how a controller keeps a cluster in shape

slides.title: An operator is a controller that runs inside the cluster

points.label: Controller
points.text: Runs in a pod and watches the resource

points.label: API server
points.text: Stores both and tells watchers what changed

copy.caveat: An operator manages only the resources it was written for.

qualifications: manages only the resources it was written for
slides.notes: Point at the cluster boundary first: everything here runs inside it.
slides.composition: Native cluster boundary holding the API server and an operator pod. The controller box is the focal node; edges show it watching the custom resource through the API server.

intent.takeaway: An operator is an ordinary controller, running in the cluster, that owns one kind of custom resource.
intent.audienceQuestion: Where does an operator run, and what does it own?
intent.rationale: Containment and the watch relationship are spatial; a diagram shows what is inside the cluster and who owns what.

alternative.reason: Cards would define the parts but hide that the controller runs inside the cluster and watches through the API server.

visual.purpose: Show what runs inside the cluster and which part owns the custom resource.

asset.description: Native nested boxes for the cluster and the operator pod, with approved Kubernetes and pod icons labelling the two actors.
asset.reason: The icons make the Kubernetes actors recognisable; the native boxes carry the containment.

slides.title: The controller closes the gap, again and again

points.label: Act
points.text: Change the cluster toward the desired state

copy.caveat: Reconciliation repeats; it is not a one-time install step.

slides.notes: Walk the loop twice: once when the resource is created, once after someone deletes a pod by hand.
slides.composition: Native row of three steps, desired state first as the focal node, with labelled edges and a curved edge from act back to observe that closes the loop.

intent.takeaway: A controller compares desired and observed state and acts on the difference, again and again.
intent.audienceQuestion: What does the controller actually do all day?
intent.rationale: The repetition is the point; a closed loop shows that acting leads back to observing.

alternative.treatment: A numbered list of three steps
alternative.reason: A list reads as a one-time sequence and loses the loop.

visual.purpose: Show desired state, observation and corrective action as one repeating loop.

asset.description: A refresh icon at the centre of the ring was considered.
asset.reason: The drawn loop already carries the repetition; an icon would decorate it without explaining anything.

slides.title: Check: a managed pod is deleted. What happens?

points.label: A
points.text: Nothing until the operator is reinstalled

points.label: B
points.text: The controller notices and recreates it

points.label: C
points.text: The custom resource is deleted too

slides.notes: Answer: B. The controller observes the drift and acts to restore the desired state.
slides.composition: Direct text: the question as the title and three lettered choices in one column, equal weight.

intent.takeaway: Learners can predict reconciliation in a concrete failure.
intent.audienceQuestion: Can I apply the loop to a real situation?
intent.rationale: A knowledge check needs the question and its choices, read as equals.

alternative.treatment: The reconciliation diagram with the deleted pod marked
alternative.reason: The diagram would show the answer before the learner chooses.

visual.purpose: Pose the question and its choices with nothing that hints at the answer.

asset.description: No asset; a question mark illustration was considered.
asset.reason: Direct text is the treatment: a graphic would add decoration or give away the answer.

slides.visibleText: Which answer is right? A, B or C
